title: Crushing chest pain at rest in a 66-year-old man with worsening angina
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 66-year-old retired painter with known angina who presents to the ED with 30 minutes of crushing central chest pain at rest that GTN has not relieved, after 3 weeks of worsening angina. The candidate then interprets his observations, 12-lead ECG, blood results and chest X-ray, makes a provisional diagnosis of unstable angina, risk stratifies him, and outlines ED management, secondary prevention and safety netting.
focus: Recognising unstable (crescendo and rest) angina from the history, and knowing that a normal ECG and an early normal troponin do not exclude an acute coronary syndrome
stem:
You are the intern in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Your next patient is Markus Ore, a 66-year-old retired painter, who has come in with chest pain. He is on a trolley in the acute area.

His observations on arrival were: BP 140/90 mmHg, heart rate 95/min, respiratory rate 15/min, temperature 36.8 °C, SpO2 97% on room air. BMI 30. He appears to be in pain and short of breath.

A nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Markus and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Act on anything the nurse tells you (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Markus's observations, his 12-lead ECG, his blood results and his chest X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Markus Ore, a 66-year-old retired painter. You are sitting up on the trolley, sweaty, a little short of breath and pressing a fist into the middle of your chest. You can talk in full sentences but you are in a lot of pain and frightened. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

Opening line: "I'm in a lot of pain..."

  • If asked to say more: "It's in my chest, but it's worse than ever before!"

History (give only when asked)

The pain today

  • Site: the middle of your chest.
  • Radiation (if asked): it goes up the left side of your neck and down your left arm.
  • Character: crushing, "like an elephant is sitting on me".
  • Severity: "11 out of 10."
  • Onset: it started about 30 minutes before you arrived, while you were sitting at home after breakfast. Your wife Martha drove you in.
  • Pattern: constant since it started, and getting worse.
  • Better or worse: nothing makes it better or worse. Breathing, moving and pressing on your chest do not change it.
  • "This one today is the longest I've had."

Previous episodes (give when asked about previous pain or what helps)

  • You have had chest pain on and off for a while (angina diagnosed 5 years ago), but it has been more frequent over the past 3 weeks. Last night you had a long episode after a walk.
  • Resting used to settle it, and so did your GTN spray. Today you used the GTN 3 times, 5 minutes apart, and it did not help at all.
  • GTN use: you used to need it once or twice a week. Recently you have needed it every day.
  • Exercise: you used to walk 1 km without stopping. Now you can barely manage 100 m.
  • Recovery: the pain sometimes carries on even when you rest, for maybe 20 to 30 minutes.

Associated symptoms

  • Yes: you are sweaty and short of breath.
  • No nausea or vomiting, no palpitations, no fainting or light-headedness.

Other causes (all negative, give only if asked)

  • The pain is not tearing or ripping, did not hit full strength in an instant, and does not go through to your back.
  • No cough, no cold or runny nose, no fever, no recent illness or sick contacts, no recent travel. No painful or swollen calf.
  • No acid reflux or heartburn, no change in your bowels.
  • No injury to your chest, no tender spot, no rash.
  • No weight loss, no unusual tiredness.

Past medical history

  • Angina for 5 years (your GP diagnosed it; you have never had a stent or an angiogram).
  • Type 2 diabetes for 10 years. You manage it with diet. Your GP has said your sugars are creeping up.
  • Osteoarthritis of the left knee for 7 years.
  • No lung problems, no anxiety or panic attacks, no reflux or stomach ulcers.
  • Not aware of high blood pressure.

Medications

  • GTN spray 400 micrograms when needed.
  • Aspirin 100 mg daily (you took it this morning).
  • Atorvastatin 40 mg daily.
  • If asked: no blood thinners, no tablets for erections (such as Viagra or Cialis), no anti-inflammatories, no supplements.

Allergies: none.

Bleeding risk (only if asked): no bleeding problems, no black stools, no stomach ulcers, no stroke, no recent operations or injuries.

Family history

  • Mum: heart attack at 57.
  • Dad: type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure.

Social history

  • You live with your wife Martha in the outer eastern suburbs.
  • Retired house painter.
  • You smoke about 10 cigarettes a day and have since you were 16 (25 pack-years).
  • About 2 beers most days. No recreational drugs.
  • Home-cooked meals with the occasional takeaway. You walk 3 times a week and sometimes play golf, though it has become harder recently because of the chest pain.
  • If asked: you are not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are terrified. Ask: "Am I having a heart attack?" Your mum had one at 57. You want the pain to stop and to know what is going on.

The nurse and how Markus changes

  • When asked, the nurse gives the arrival observations (10:02) as in the stem, and BGL 9.4 mmol/L.
  • If the candidate asks for an ECG, the nurse says: "I recorded one at 10:08." The examiner says it will be given in Part 2. If asked for IV access and bloods, the nurse says: "Cannula's in and bloods are off at 10:10, including a troponin."
  • If the candidate orders a medicine, a chest X-ray or a senior review, the nurse says: "Will do." The examiner notes it for marking in Part 2.
  • About 6 minutes into Part 1 (or as the examination starts, if sooner), the nurse says: "Doctor, he's still in a lot of pain and he's sweaty. Repeat obs: BP 146/92, heart rate 98, resps 18, sats 97% on room air."
  • If no pain relief has been ordered by then, Markus says: "Doc, can you give me something? It's getting worse."
  • If the candidate gives sublingual GTN (after checking the BP), the pain eases only slightly, to about 9/10. If they order a titrated IV opioid, by the end of Part 1 the pain is about 6/10 and Markus is calmer. It does not go away completely.
  • If the candidate explains what they are doing in plain words, Markus settles a little and thanks them.

Exam findings

  • General: overweight man (BMI 30), pale and sweaty, in obvious pain, mildly short of breath but speaking in full sentences. Tar staining of the right index and middle fingers. No xanthelasma.
  • Vital signs: as in the nurse's 10:20 repeat set.
  • Pulse: 98/min, regular, normal volume. Radial pulses equal, no radio-radial or radio-femoral delay.
  • Blood pressure: right arm 146/92 mmHg, left arm 144/90 mmHg.
  • Perfusion: peripheries warm, CRT 2 seconds.
  • JVP: not raised.
  • Heart: apex beat not displaced. Dual heart sounds, no added sounds, no murmurs (no ejection systolic murmur), no pericardial rub.
  • Chest wall: not tender; pressing does not reproduce the pain.
  • Lungs: trachea central, equal expansion, resonant, vesicular breath sounds, no crackles or wheeze.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender, no epigastric tenderness, no pulsatile mass.
  • Legs: calves soft and non-tender, no swelling, no ankle oedema. Peripheral pulses present. Crepitus in the left knee.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as the intern and confirms Markus's identity.

Recognises a possible acute coronary syndrome from the start: asks the nurse for continuous cardiac monitoring, confirms a 12-lead ECG has been done (or requests one) and asks to see it now, IV access and bloods including a troponin, and keeps the history focused.
Acknowledges his pain and fear ("Am I having a heart attack?") with empathy, offers pain relief early and uses plain language.
History
Characterises today's chest pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: central, to the left side of the neck and down the left arm
Character and severity: crushing, 'like an elephant sitting on me', 11/10
Onset and time course: started at rest about 30 minutes before arrival, constant and worsening, the longest he has had
Relieving factors: nothing helps, including GTN 3 times 5 minutes apart

check.x: Establishes how his angina has changed (assessment of severity):

kids.x: Episodes more frequent over the past 3 weeks, with a prolonged episode last night after a walk
GTN use up from once or twice a week to every day
Exercise tolerance down from 1 km to barely 100 m
Episodes now continue at rest for 20 to 30 minutes

check.x: Asks about associated cardiovascular symptoms: sweating and breathlessness (present), nausea or vomiting, palpitations and syncope (absent).
Asks cluster questions for the other causes of chest pain:

kids.x: Aortic dissection: tearing pain, maximal at onset, radiating to the back
Respiratory and PE: cough, coryza, fever, sick contacts, travel, calf pain or swelling
GI: reflux or heartburn, change in bowels
Musculoskeletal and skin: chest trauma or tenderness, rash; and constitutional symptoms (weight loss, fatigue)

check.x: Asks about cardiovascular risk factors, including smoking (quantified) and diabetes, and the family history of premature coronary disease: current smoker 25 pack-years, type 2 diabetes, BMI 30, hypercholesterolaemia on a statin; mother had an MI at 57, father has diabetes and hypertension.
check.d: Award if the candidate asks about smoking (quantified), diabetes and at least one other risk factor or the family history of premature CAD.

check.x: Takes the past history, medications and allergies: angina 5 years, type 2 diabetes 10 years (diet), left knee osteoarthritis, no respiratory, psychiatric or GORD history; GTN 400 microgram spray, aspirin 100 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg; no allergies.

Checks for contraindications before antithrombotics and nitrates: bleeding history, peptic ulcer, stroke, recent surgery, anticoagulant use, and a PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil) in the last 24 to 48 hours.
Takes a focused social history: alcohol (2 beers most days), occupation, home and supports (lives with wife Martha), diet and exercise, and asks about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status.
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: he fears a heart attack (his mother had one at 57) and wants the pain to stop.
Examination
General inspection and review of the vital signs: pale, sweaty, distressed, mildly breathless, tar-stained fingers, BMI 30.
Compares the radial pulses and the BP in both arms (equal) to look for aortic dissection.
Cardiovascular examination: perfusion (CRT, peripheral temperature), JVP, heart sounds, murmurs (including the ejection systolic murmur of aortic stenosis), a third heart sound and a pericardial rub.
Respiratory examination for the crackles of heart failure and signs of pneumothorax or consolidation.
Palpates the chest wall (not tender), examines the abdomen and checks the calves and ankles for DVT and oedema.

Responds to the nurse's report of ongoing severe pain: reassesses him and orders analgesia (sublingual GTN after checking SBP above 90 and no PDE5 inhibitor, and a titrated IV opioid) and asks for a repeat ECG or senior review.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: every vital sign in the white zone at 10:02 and 10:20, haemodynamically stable and not hypoxic (no oxygen needed), but severe ongoing pain (charted 10/10; he says 11/10) and nurse concern are additional criteria for clinical review on the chart, so he needs immediate medical review and treatment.

Reads the ECG as sinus rhythm 92/min with no ST elevation or depression, no T wave inversion and no Q waves, unchanged from 2024, and states that a normal ECG does not exclude ACS and must be repeated (with any change in pain, or every 15 to 30 minutes while pain continues).
States that the hs-troponin of 4 ng/L is below the 99th percentile but was taken only about 40 minutes after onset, so it cannot exclude myocardial infarction, and a repeat troponin is needed.
check.d: Accept a repeat hs-troponin at 2 to 3 hours from presentation, or at the interval in the local hs-troponin pathway (for example a 0/1 h or 0/2 h algorithm). Do not accept 6 to 8 hours for this high-sensitivity assay.

check.x: Interprets the other bloods: poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c 7.9%), LDL 2.6 above the secondary prevention target on his statin, and normal Hb, platelets, coagulation and renal function (safe for antithrombotics, enoxaparin and angiography).
check.d: Accept a target of below 1.8 or below 1.4 mmol/L.

check.x: Interprets the chest X-ray as normal: no widened mediastinum, pneumothorax, pulmonary oedema or consolidation.

Gives unstable angina as the provisional diagnosis, justified by ongoing rest pain with sweating and breathlessness unrelieved by GTN, on a background of crescendo angina over 3 weeks and multiple risk factors, with no ST elevation (not a STEMI) and a normal first troponin taken too early to exclude NSTEMI, so unstable angina is provisional until serial troponins stay normal.
check.d: Accept "NSTEACS: likely unstable angina, NSTEMI not excluded until the repeat troponin". Do not accept "angina" or "ACS" with no further qualification.

check.x: Gives differentials with a feature for or against each: NSTEMI (not excluded until the repeat troponin), aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, and GORD or oesophageal spasm.
Risk stratifies him as very high risk because ischaemic pain is ongoing despite nitrates and opioid (also not low risk: prolonged rest pain, diabetes, known CAD).
check.d: Also accept: not low risk now; very high risk (angiography within 2 hours) if pain persists despite IV GTN. Do not accept low risk.

check.x: Management
Gives aspirin 300 mg chewed or dispersed now, even though he takes 100 mg daily, after checking allergy and bleeding risk.

Treats the pain: sublingual GTN 400 microgram every 5 minutes up to 3 doses if SBP above 90 mmHg, then IV GTN infusion if pain persists, titrated IV opioid (e.g. fentanyl 25–50 microgram IV or morphine 2.5–5 mg IV) with an antiemetic if needed; no oxygen while SpO2 is 93% or above.

Calls the cardiology registrar now and gives a P2Y12 inhibitor (for example ticagrelor 180 mg loading) and parenteral anticoagulation (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC 12-hourly or IV heparin) as cardiology directs.
Angiography within 2 hours (very high risk: ongoing pain despite treatment); if pain fully settles on IV GTN, within 72 hours (intermediate risk: diabetes).
check.d: Credit a stress test before discharge only if the candidate names it as the route when cardiology chooses non-invasive assessment.

check.x: Admits him (not for discharge from ED) with continuous ECG monitoring, serial ECGs and troponins, and investigation of the worsening angina before discharge.
check.d: Accept CCU or a monitored cardiology bed (telemetry), or the cath lab for very high risk (ongoing pain). Do not accept an ED short-stay or chest pain unit while he has ongoing pain or diabetes as an intermediate-risk feature.

check.x: Plans anti-anginal treatment and secondary prevention: a beta blocker if no contraindication (or a long-acting nitrate) and atorvastatin 80 mg, with smoking cessation, diabetes review and a cardiac rehabilitation referral.
check.d: Award for the beta blocker (or long-acting nitrate) and high-intensity statin plus at least one of smoking cessation, diabetes review or cardiac rehabilitation referral.

check.x: Safety netting

Tells Markus in plain words that this looks like a serious warning sign of a heart attack, that the heart arteries need to be checked in hospital, and to tell a nurse straight away about worse or returning pain, breathlessness, feeling faint, palpitations or any bleeding.

Gives a chest pain action plan for home: stop and rest, use GTN and repeat after 5 minutes, call 000 if the pain is severe, getting worse or lasts 10 minutes, and do not drive himself or be driven to hospital.

part2.lead: Here are Markus's observations, his 12-lead ECG, his blood results and his chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
When the candidate explains what is happening, ask:

  • "So is it a heart attack or not?"

You are relieved if the candidate explains clearly that the tests so far do not show a heart attack but the pain is a serious warning sign. If they use jargon such as "troponin" or "unstable angina", ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result:
Room air throughout. Arrival set at 10:02; the nurse repeated the set at 10:20 because of ongoing pain. Any medicines ordered in Part 1 had not yet taken effect at 10:20.

Update at 10:40: after sublingual GTN and IV morphine (or fentanyl) given in the ED, pain is 6/10 and persisting; an IV GTN infusion is being started.
handover.model:
• Read: at 10:02 RR 15, SpO2 97% on room air, BP 140/90, HR 95 regular, temperature 36.8 °C, alert, BGL 9.4: all white zone. At 10:20 RR 18, BP 146/92, HR 98: still white zone. Pain 10/10 at both times: severe ongoing pain and nurse concern are additional criteria for clinical review on the chart.
  • Meaning: haemodynamically stable, not hypoxic, no signs of heart failure or shock, but ongoing severe ischaemic-type pain with a rising HR and BP. At 10:40 the pain persists at 6/10 despite GTN and IV opioid: ongoing ischaemia despite treatment.
  • Changes: no rapid response trigger, but severe pain and a worried nurse call for immediate medical review: analgesia and nitrates now, repeat ECG, continuous monitoring. No oxygen at SpO2 97%. Ongoing pain despite nitrates and opioid makes him very high risk: cardiology now for angiography within 2 hours.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: chest pain, GTN x3 at home without relief; ECG requested
Still in severe pain, sweaty; doctor informed

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG: Markus Ore, 66-year-old man, recorded at 10:08 in the ED during ongoing chest pain (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: 92/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus rhythm, regular, a P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about +40°.
  • P waves: normal morphology.
  • PR interval: 170 ms.
  • QRS: 94 ms, normal morphology, no pathological Q waves, normal R wave progression, no bundle branch block, no LVH by voltage criteria.
  • QTc: 430 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments: isoelectric in all leads. No ST elevation and no ST depression, including V1 to V3.
  • T waves: upright in I, II, III, aVL, aVF and V2 to V6, inverted in aVR (normal), upright in V1; no T wave inversion or hyperacute T waves.
  • Comparison: GP ECG from March 2024 on file; no change.
handover.model:
• Read: checks the patient and time (10:08, recorded during pain). Sinus rhythm 92/min, normal axis, PR, QRS and QTc. No ST elevation or depression, no T inversion, no Q waves, no bundle branch block. Unchanged from 2024.
  • Meaning: no STEMI and no ischaemic changes, but a normal ECG during pain does not exclude ACS; many patients with NSTEACS have a normal or non-diagnostic first ECG, and circumflex territory ischaemia can be electrically silent.
  • Changes: not for the STEMI pathway. Repeat the ECG every 15 to 30 minutes while pain continues and with any change in symptoms; consider posterior leads (V7 to V9). Dynamic changes would make him high or very high risk.

handover.label: Bloods
handover.result: Venous sample collected 10:10 from the IV cannula, about 40 minutes after pain onset. Lipids non-fasting. Repeat hs-troponin due per ED protocol.
handover.model:
• Read: hs-troponin I 4 ng/L, below the 99th percentile (26), but taken about 40 minutes after onset. Random glucose 9.6 and HbA1c 7.9% (63 mmol/mol) are high. LDL 2.6 is above the target of below 1.8 (or below 1.4) on his statin, HDL low and triglycerides high. Hb, WCC, platelets, electrolytes, magnesium, renal function and coagulation are normal.
  • Meaning: no evidence of myocardial injury yet, but one early troponin cannot exclude NSTEMI. His diabetes is poorly controlled on diet alone and his lipids are not at secondary prevention target.
  • Changes: repeat troponin (2 to 3 hours per the hs-troponin protocol; 6 to 8 hours with older assays). Normal Hb, platelets and coagulation show no contraindication to antithrombotics, and normal renal function means no dose adjustment for enoxaparin and a low contrast risk. Increase atorvastatin to 80 mg; review diabetes treatment.

rows.n: about 40 minutes after pain onset; repeat due

handover.label: Chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, portable AP erect, 10:30.

Clinical details: 66-year-old man, smoker, with ongoing central chest pain and breathlessness. ?Mediastinal widening ?pulmonary oedema ?pneumothorax.

Findings:

  • Lines and devices: ECG electrodes over the chest. No lines or tubes.
  • Lungs: clear. No consolidation, collapse or mass. No pulmonary oedema; normal pulmonary vasculature.
  • Pleura: no pneumothorax and no pleural effusion. Costophrenic angles sharp.
  • Heart and mediastinum: heart size within normal limits for an AP film. Mediastinum not widened, normal aortic contour. Trachea central, hila normal.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no acute bony abnormality. Mild degenerative change in the thoracic spine.

Conclusion: no acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.
handover.model:
• Read: adequate AP film: clear lungs, no oedema, no pneumothorax or effusion, normal heart size for an AP film, mediastinum not widened, no mass.
  • Meaning: no heart failure, which keeps him out of the very high-risk group on this criterion; no pneumothorax or pneumonia; a normal mediastinum, with equal arm BPs and non-tearing pain, makes aortic dissection unlikely before antithrombotics (a normal film does not fully exclude it).
  • Changes: nothing on the film delays aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulation or angiography.

ask: You are now calling the cardiology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Markus Ore, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Markus now, here in the emergency department.
Markus asks what is happening. Explain it to him, tell him what to report while he is in hospital, and give him his chest pain action plan for when he goes home.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Markus Ore, 66.
  • Situation: crushing central chest pain at rest for over 30 minutes, to left neck and arm, 10/10, sweaty and breathless, unrelieved by GTN x3; still 6/10 at 10:40 despite GTN and IV opioid, IV GTN starting.
  • Background: angina 5 years, crescendo for 3 weeks (daily GTN, 100 m, rest episodes of 20 to 30 min); diet-controlled T2DM, smoker 25 pack-years, BMI 30, mother MI at 57; aspirin, atorvastatin; no allergies or bleeding risk.
  • Assessment: obs white zone, pain severe and ongoing. ECG sinus 92, no ischaemic changes, unchanged. hs-troponin 4 at 40 minutes, too early to exclude MI. HbA1c 7.9% (poorly controlled), LDL 2.6 above target on statin. Hb, platelets, coags and renal function normal: safe for antithrombotics and angiography. CXR normal. Likely unstable angina, very high risk (ongoing pain despite treatment).
  • Recommendation: please review now for angiography within 2 hours; advise on P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulation; admit under cardiology.

Unstable angina: ongoing rest pain over 20 minutes with sweating and breathlessness, unrelieved by GTN, after 3 weeks of crescendo angina, with multiple risk factors; normal ECG and troponin so far.

  • NSTEMI: for: same picture; against: troponin normal, but only 40 minutes after onset, so not excluded until the repeat.
  • Aortic dissection: against: not tearing, no back pain, equal arm BPs, normal mediastinum.
  • Pulmonary embolism: for: breathlessness; against: no calf symptoms or travel, SpO2 97%, not pleuritic.
  • GORD or oesophageal spasm: against: no reflux, exertional pattern, radiation to neck and arm.

1. Continuous monitoring, repeat ECG every 15 to 30 minutes while in pain; no oxygen (SpO2 97%).
  2. Aspirin 300 mg chewed now.
  3. Sublingual GTN 400 microgram every 5 minutes up to 3 doses if SBP above 90 (no PDE5 inhibitor), then IV GTN infusion; titrated IV opioid (e.g. fentanyl 25–50 microgram IV or morphine 2.5–5 mg IV, titrated every 5 minutes to effect) with an antiemetic.
  4. Cardiology now: P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor 180 mg) and enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC 12-hourly or IV heparin as directed.
  5. Ongoing pain despite nitrates and opioid = very high risk: angiography within 2 hours. If pain fully settles on IV GTN: within 72 hours (intermediate risk: diabetes); admit under cardiology.
  6. Repeat troponin; serial ECGs.
  7. Plan: beta blocker, atorvastatin 80 mg, nicotine replacement, diabetes review, cardiac rehabilitation referral.

• Explanation: the heart arteries are narrowed and the pain is a warning sign of a heart attack; tests so far show no damage.
  • In hospital: tell a nurse straight away about worse or returning pain, breathlessness, feeling faint, palpitations or any bleeding.
  • Action plan: stop and rest, use GTN, repeat after 5 minutes; call 000 if the pain is severe, getting worse or lasts 10 minutes. Do not drive or be driven to hospital.

ddx.for: Crushing central rest pain for over 30 minutes to the left neck and arm, unrelieved by 3 GTN doses, after 3 weeks of more frequent, longer and lower-threshold angina, with diabetes, smoking and a mother with an MI at 57.
ddx.against: Nothing against it yet, but it is a provisional diagnosis until serial troponins stay normal.

ddx.for: The same ongoing ischaemic pain with sweating and breathlessness in a man with known coronary disease.
ddx.against: His hs-troponin is 4 ng/L and the ECG is normal, although the troponin was taken only about 40 minutes after onset.

ddx.for: Severe central chest pain in a 66-year-old smoker with a BP of 146/92 at the repeat set.
ddx.against: The pain is crushing rather than tearing, built up rather than maximal at onset, does not go to the back, the arm BPs are equal and the mediastinum is normal.
No calf pain or swelling, no travel or immobility, the pain is not pleuritic and SpO2 is 97% on room air.

ddx.for: Oesophageal spasm can cause crushing pain that responds variably to nitrates.
ddx.against: No reflux history, the episodes are exertional and the pain radiates to the neck and left arm with sweating.

guide:
In Part 1, Markus answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. The nurse gives the arrival observations when asked. If the candidate asks for the ECG, bloods or chest X-ray, say they will be given in Part 2 (in practice the ECG would be read within 10 minutes). About 6 minutes in, the nurse reports ongoing pain with the 10:20 observations; mark the bedside response (item 21) in Part 1. Medicines or calls ordered in Part 1 are noted and credited against the Management items in Part 2.

In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order (about 75 seconds each). Question 4 is brief: explanation, in-hospital red flags and the GTN/000 action plan only. Read Markus's Part 2 question during question 4. Do not accept just "angina" or "acute coronary syndrome" with no further qualification for the diagnosis: the candidate must say unstable angina (or NSTEACS, likely unstable angina, with NSTEMI not yet excluded) and justify it.

Do not credit discharge from ED, short-stay admission or a 6 to 8 hour troponin with this hs-assay. Markus is not low risk (prolonged rest pain, diabetes, known coronary disease), and the 10:40 update shows his pain persisting despite nitrates and opioid, which makes him very high risk for angiography within 2 hours. Accept troponin timing per a local hs-troponin protocol (2 to 3 hours). A candidate who would discharge him once the troponin is normal fails item 36.

A high-performing candidate asks for monitoring and an ECG in the first minute, characterises the pain and how the angina has changed (GTN use, exercise tolerance, rest episodes), screens for dissection and other causes, checks bleeding risk and PDE5 inhibitors, and treats the pain when the nurse reports it. In Part 2 they say the ECG is normal but does not exclude ACS, that one early troponin cannot rule out MI, name unstable angina, give aspirin 300 mg and nitrates, involve cardiology for a P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulation, and know the angiography timeframes.

A borderline candidate takes a long, unfocused history without the change in angina pattern, misses dissection or bleeding risk, ignores the ongoing pain, reads a normal ECG and troponin as reassurance to send him home, or gives routine oxygen.
explain:
Diagnosis: unstable angina

Markus has known stable angina that has become unstable. For 3 weeks his episodes have been more frequent, he needs GTN daily instead of once or twice a week, his walking distance has fallen from 1 km to 100 m, and episodes now go on at rest for 20 to 30 minutes. Today he has crushing central pain at rest, radiating to the left neck and arm, with sweating and breathlessness, and 3 doses of GTN have not helped. His ECG is normal and his first troponin is not raised. That is unstable angina, part of the spectrum of non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTEACS). Unstable angina presents in three ways: rest angina (usually lasting over 20 minutes), new-onset severe angina, and crescendo angina, which is more frequent, longer or brought on by less exertion. He has crescendo angina and rest pain. He also has many risk factors: current smoker of 25 pack-years, diabetes for 10 years, obesity, hypercholesterolaemia, and a mother who had an MI at 57.

Unstable angina is ischaemia without myocardial necrosis, so it can only be called once serial troponins stay normal. With high-sensitivity assays, many patients once labelled unstable angina are found to have a small NSTEMI. "Angina" or "ACS" alone is not an adequate answer.

Priorities in suspected ACS

Assessment is the same whether this turns out to be unstable angina, NSTEMI or STEMI. First make sure he is stable, then investigate, then risk stratify. A STEMI needs urgent reperfusion. Unstable angina and NSTEMI are stabilised, investigated and risk stratified to decide how quickly angiography is needed. The ECG should be recorded and read within 10 minutes of first medical contact.

The focused history

Characterise the pain, then measure how severe the angina has become: GTN use, exercise tolerance and how long episodes take to settle. Screen the other systems: dissection (tearing pain, worst at onset, back pain), PE and respiratory causes, GI causes, and chest wall causes. Before giving antithrombotics or nitrates, ask about bleeding, ulcers, stroke, recent surgery, anticoagulants and PDE5 inhibitors. The examination looks for shock, heart failure, a murmur (aortic stenosis can cause angina), signs of dissection (unequal arm BPs or pulses) and other causes.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: all white zone, so he is haemodynamically stable, but severe ongoing pain and a concerned nurse call for immediate review. Oxygen is not given when SpO2 is 93% or above. At 10:40 his pain persists at 6/10 despite GTN and IV opioid.
  • ECG: normal and unchanged. A normal ECG during pain does not exclude ACS. Repeat it every 15 to 30 minutes while pain continues and with any change in symptoms, and consider posterior leads, because circumflex ischaemia can be electrically silent.
  • Troponin: 4 ng/L at about 40 minutes after onset is too early to exclude MI. Repeat it according to the local hs-troponin protocol (usually 2 to 3 hours with high-sensitivity assays; 6 to 8 hours was standard with older assays). A rise and/or fall above the 99th percentile would mean NSTEMI.
  • Other bloods: HbA1c 7.9% shows poorly controlled diabetes; LDL 2.6 mmol/L is above the secondary prevention target of below 1.8 mmol/L on his statin (many cardiologists now aim for below 1.4 mmol/L after ACS); normal Hb, platelets and coagulation show no contraindication to antithrombotics, and normal renal function means no enoxaparin dose adjustment and a low contrast risk for angiography.
  • Chest X-ray: no heart failure, pneumothorax or widened mediastinum.

Risk stratification (Heart Foundation 2016)

His ongoing prolonged rest pain and diabetes with typical symptoms mean he is not low risk and must not be discharged from the ED. Once NSTEACS is confirmed, the guideline sets the timing of angiography by risk. Very high risk includes recurrent or ongoing ischaemia that does not respond to medical treatment, haemodynamic instability, heart failure or life-threatening arrhythmia, and needs angiography within 2 hours. High risk (a troponin rise or fall, dynamic ST or T changes, or GRACE above 140) needs it within 24 hours. Intermediate risk, which includes diabetes, needs it within 72 hours. Markus's pain persists despite nitrates and opioid, so he meets the very high-risk criterion of ongoing ischaemia despite medical treatment (and certainly if pain persists on IV GTN) and needs angiography within 2 hours; if the pain fully settled on IV GTN, his diabetes would still make him intermediate risk (within 72 hours).

Management

  • Continuous monitoring, IV access, serial ECGs and troponins. Oxygen only if SpO2 is below 93%.
  • Aspirin 300 mg chewed or dispersed, even if he already takes daily aspirin.
  • Sublingual GTN 400 microgram every 5 minutes up to 3 doses if SBP is above 90 mmHg and no PDE5 inhibitor has been taken, then IV GTN if pain continues. Give a titrated IV opioid for ongoing pain (e.g. fentanyl 25–50 microgram IV or morphine 2.5–5 mg IV, titrated every 5 minutes to effect), with an antiemetic if needed, and IV fluids only if needed. Opioids (morphine and fentanyl) slow gut transit and can delay oral P2Y12 inhibitor absorption; use the lowest effective titrated dose.
  • Cardiology involvement now. A P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor is preferred in intermediate- to high-risk NSTEACS) and parenteral anticoagulation (enoxaparin or unfractionated heparin) as the cardiology team directs.
  • Admit with monitoring and investigate the worsening angina. In a patient who is not low risk this usually means coronary angiography. Stress or functional testing before discharge is used when a non-invasive approach is chosen.

Anti-anginal treatment and secondary prevention (eTG)

A beta blocker is first-line anti-anginal therapy if there is no contraindication (he has no bradycardia, heart failure or asthma). A long-acting nitrate or a calcium channel blocker can be added or substituted. Increase his statin to high-intensity (atorvastatin 80 mg), given an LDL above target. Continue aspirin, with dual antiplatelet therapy as cardiology advises after the ACS. Optimise diabetes control, help him stop smoking (nicotine replacement in hospital, Quitline), and give weight, alcohol and exercise advice. Everyone after an ACS should be referred to cardiac rehabilitation.

Safety netting and follow-up

In hospital, he should tell a nurse at once about returning or worse pain, breathlessness, faintness or palpitations, and he will have a repeat ECG with any pain. At home he needs a written chest pain action plan: stop and rest, take GTN, repeat after 5 minutes if needed, and call 000 if the pain is severe, getting worse or lasts 10 minutes. He should not drive himself or be driven to hospital, as he was today. Follow-up is cardiology review, GP review within 1 to 2 weeks for diabetes, lipids and blood pressure, cardiac rehabilitation and Quitline.
points: Unstable angina is rest angina (usually over 20 minutes), new severe angina or crescendo angina. Measure the change: GTN use, exercise tolerance and how long episodes take to settle.
A normal ECG does not exclude ACS. Repeat it every 15 to 30 minutes while pain continues and with any change in symptoms.
One early hs-troponin, taken soon after pain onset, cannot exclude MI. Unstable angina is only confirmed when serial troponins stay normal; a rise and/or fall above the 99th percentile means NSTEMI.
Give aspirin 300 mg, nitrates (if SBP above 90 mmHg and no PDE5 inhibitor) and titrated opioid. Give oxygen only if SpO2 is below 93%. Agree the P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulation with cardiology.

Heart Foundation risk stratification: ongoing ischaemia that does not respond to treatment is very high risk (angiography within 2 hours). Diabetes and prolonged rest pain mean the patient is not low risk, so he is not discharged from the ED.
Before discharge: a GTN action plan with 000 at 10 minutes, a beta blocker, a high-intensity statin, help to stop smoking, better diabetes control and cardiac rehabilitation.
